items.summary: This Notice announces changes in the interest rates to be paid on debentures issued with respect to a loan or mortgage insured by the Federal Housing Administration under the provisions of the National Housing Act (the Act). The interest rate for debentures issued under any other provision of the Act is the rate in effect on the date that the commitment to insure the loan or mortgage was issued, or the date that the loan or mortgage was endorsed (or initially endorsed if there are two or more endorsements) for insurance, whichever rate is higher. The interest rate for debentures issued under these other provisions with respect to a loan or mortgage committed or endorsed during the 6-month period beginning July 1, 2026, is 5 percent.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Continuing care retirement communities and assisted living employment, October 2026 — 1,021.60 thousands of jobs (+0.5% year over year)
story_ideas.headline: Senior living added almost no staff this year
story_ideas.angle: A straight read of the October CCRC and assisted living employment line, 1,021.60 thousands of jobs and up 0.5% in twelve months, for operators and for families touring buildings.
story_ideas.hook: Half a percent of growth in a year, against 4.4% in home health care services, in the setting families are most often sold on staffing.
story_ideas.consumer: When you tour a community, ask how many caregiving and dining positions are open today and how that compares with a year ago, and ask what share of shifts are filled by agency staff.
story_ideas.b2b: If headcount is flat while wages rise, the constraint on move-ins is labor supply rather than demand, which changes what an occupancy forecast is worth.
story_ideas.why: A building that cannot grow its staff cannot absorb a resident whose needs grow, and you find that out after you move in unless you ask first.
story_ideas.note: National series only, but charts cleanly against the home health and nursing facility lines; coverage is light rather than absent.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Assisted living and CCRC average hourly earnings, September 2026 — 25.99 dollars per hour (+5.4% year over year)
story_ideas.headline: The raise is real and it still trails home care pay
story_ideas.angle: The fastest wage growth of any long-term care setting, 5.4% to $25.99 an hour, set against home health's $28.26, for senior living finance and operations readers.
story_ideas.hook: Senior living gave the biggest percentage raise in the sector and still pays $2.27 an hour less than home health.
story_ideas.consumer: If your monthly fee went up this year, the wage line is part of the reason, and you can ask the community what share of the increase went to direct care pay.
story_ideas.b2b: Model what a 5.4% wage increase that yields 0.5% employment growth does to labor cost per resident day before next year's rate letters go out.
story_ideas.why: You are paying for staffing you may not be getting, and the pay gap tells you where the workers went.
story_ideas.note: Wage series runs a month behind employment; pairs with the October headcount print for a two-panel chart.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Home health care services employment, October 2026 — 1,903.60 thousands of jobs (+4.4% year over year)
story_ideas.headline: Home care is hiring faster than any other way of growing old
story_ideas.angle: The October home health figure of 1,903.60 thousands of jobs, up 4.4%, read as a supply signal for anyone planning to age in place.
story_ideas.hook: The sector adding staff fastest is the one that comes to the house, not the one that houses you.
story_ideas.consumer: If you are deciding between moving and staying put, the hiring numbers favor staying put, so get on an agency's list and ask how far out their scheduling runs.
story_ideas.b2b: Home health's hiring advantage is being bought with slower raises, which is a recruiting argument congregate operators can use and are not using.
story_ideas.chart: The underlying file supports an original ranking or trend line.
story_ideas.competitive: Monitored trades cover this beat and have not written it.
story_ideas.why: Whether help can be found at all is the first question behind aging in place, and this is the only national measure of it that updates monthly.
story_ideas.note: Confirmed gap against monitored publishers; localizable framing possible using the national trend as a benchmark.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Home health care services average hourly earnings, September 2026 — 28.26 dollars per hour (+2.5% year over year)
story_ideas.headline: $28.26 an hour is what home care pays the person who shows up
story_ideas.angle: The September home health wage print, up 2.5%, measured against what agencies bill families, for readers buying care privately.
story_ideas.hook: Pay rose 2.5% while the workforce grew 4.4%, which is an unusual combination and worth explaining.
story_ideas.consumer: When an agency quotes you an hourly rate, ask what share of it reaches the aide, and compare the answer with the $28.26 national average.
story_ideas.b2b: Slow wage growth alongside fast headcount growth suggests home health is recruiting on availability of hours rather than on price.
story_ideas.why: Knowing the going wage is the only leverage you have in a private-pay negotiation.
story_ideas.note: Confirmed gap; national figure, best used as the benchmark line in a local cost story.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Employment level, 65 years and over, October 2026 — 11,862 thousands of people
story_ideas.headline: Nearly 12 million Americans over 65 are still on the clock
story_ideas.angle: The October level of 11,862 thousands of people aged 65 and over, for retirement-finance readers deciding when to stop.
story_ideas.hook: The count moved up sharply from the September print of 11,654 thousands carried in our 11/02 run.
story_ideas.consumer: If you are working past 65, check how your earnings interact with your benefits and coverage choices before you add hours.
story_ideas.b2b: Senior living and home care employers recruit from this same cohort, and a rising older-worker count is a staffing pool, not just a retirement statistic.
story_ideas.why: The decision to keep working is usually made alone, and this is the number that shows how many people are making it.
story_ideas.note: Confirmed gap; monthly series with obvious chart potential over a twelve-month window.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Nursing care facilities employment, October 2026 — 1,591.80 thousands of jobs (+2.1% year over year)
story_ideas.headline: Nursing homes are rehiring, slowly

story_ideas.b2b: A sector growing 2.1% while competing against a sector growing 4.4% should expect its agency spend to stay where it is.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** The October employment print pulls long-term care apart into three labor markets that are no longer moving together. Home health care services reached 1,903.60 thousands of jobs in October 2026, up 4.4% year over year, on average hourly earnings of $28.26 in September, up 2.5%. Continuing care retirement communities and assisted living sat at 1,021.60 thousands of jobs, up 0.5% over twelve months, while paying 5.4% more, at $25.99 an hour. Nursing care facilities landed in between at 1,591.80 thousands of jobs, up 2.1%. Read together, those three BLS series say congregate care is buying raises it cannot convert into headcount, while home-based care is adding people four times faster on slower pay increases.

**Why it matters:** A family choosing assisted living is choosing the setting whose workforce grew half a percent in a year, and whose average wage sits $2.27 an hour below what home health pays, while the two settings recruit from the same pool. For operators, a 5.4% wage increase that produces 0.5% employment growth is money spent holding position. The 11,862 thousands of people aged 65 and over who were working in October are part of the same labor market, not separate from it.

**Why pitch this now:** All six of these series were first collected in this run, the October employment figures are the newest print available, and the September wage figures are the most recent wage data. The home health and nursing care facility series are confirmed gaps against monitored publishers. The CY 2027 rate-setting cycle is in print alongside them, with the Medicare Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment and Ambulatory Surgical Center final rule published 11/06/26.

**Angle:** Whether congregate senior living can pay its way out of a hiring problem that home-based care is solving with volume, written as "The $2.27 Gap," for senior living and skilled nursing operators and for families weighing a building against care at home.

**Potential headlines:**
- Assisted living is paying 5.4 percent more and barely adding anyone
- Home care hired four times faster than senior living this year
- The aide who would have staffed your parent's building took a home visit job instead

**Potential outlets:**
- **Senior Housing News** — its operator readership is making 2027 labor budgets against exactly the CCRC and assisted living series that moved 0.5% on a 5.4% raise.
- **McKnight's Long-Term Care News** — the nursing care facility line at 1,591.80 thousands of jobs, up 2.1%, is the staffing number its skilled nursing audience is measured by.
- **Skilled Nursing News** — frames the same three series as a competition for workers with business consequences for census and agency spend.
- **Next Avenue** — the consumer version, for readers deciding whether the care they want is better staffed at home than in a building.
